summary: A 1970 note on padding by Steve Crocker. It is updated by RFC 228. Padding means extra filler bits added to messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This note explains how to find the one bit in a padding pattern and determine its position. It shows a bitwise method for isolating the bit and a lookup-table method for locating it.

subtitle: Bit operations and lookup tables for finding the padding bit in a word.

tldr.problem: Padding has a one bit followed by zeros, and programs need to find the position of that one within a machine word.
tldr.mechanism: The note isolates the low-order one with W AND -W and describes using a divisor and lookup table to map a remainder to the bit position.
tldr.outcome: RFC 70 is a programming note that was updated by RFC 228.

sections.title: Finding the Padding Bit
sections.content:
The note describes message padding as a string of the form 10*: a one bit followed by zero or more zero bits. Depending on the host word length, the one bit may be in the last received word or the previous word. The programming task is to find the position of that one bit.

One method repeatedly tests the low-order bit and shifts the word right when that bit is zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The padding pattern contains one marker bit followed by zeros. A program needs to find where that marker sits in the word.

sections.title: Isolating a Single Set Bit
sections.content: Assuming two's complement arithmetic, the expression W AND -W isolates the low-order one bit of a nonzero word W. The expression W AND W-1 instead removes that bit. The note focuses on using the isolated bit to determine its position.
sections.plainLanguage: A bitwise operation can clear all other bits and leave only the lowest set bit. Another related operation removes that bit from the original word.

sections.title: Using a Remainder Lookup Table
sections.content:
A word containing only one set bit has an unsigned value of 2^k, where k is its bit position. If a divisor p gives a distinct remainder for each relevant power of two, a table can map each remainder back to k. The note gives an example using a word length of 8 and divisor 11.

The divisor should be small to keep the table short, but it must generate enough distinct remainders. The RFC lists useful divisors and includes a Fortran program that generated the table.
sections.plainLanguage: After isolating the bit, divide its value by a chosen number. A table uses the remainder to identify the bit's position.
